name: Neo-Grünfeld Defense
summary: The Neo-Grünfeld meets White's g3/Bg2 fianchetto with an early ...d5, blending Grünfeld counterattack and King's-Indian-fianchetto ideas.
intro: The Neo-Grünfeld arises after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 d5, where Black strikes in the centre with ...d5 against White's fianchetto setup instead of facing 3.Nc3. The g2-bishop rakes the long diagonal, and the play centres on the tension between White's pieces and Black's active challenge to the c4 and d5 squares.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By playing ...d5 before White commits a knight to c3, Black steers the game into a Grünfeld-style structure with a fianchetto twist. The absence of Nc3 changes the character of the fight: White relies on the g2-bishop and piece play rather than an early pawn front, while Black seeks to pressure the centre and generate the dynamic counterattack typical of the Grünfeld.

Play revolves around the central tension. After cxd5, Black may recapture with the knight and later challenge White's centre with ...c5 or ...Nc6, or the tension can persist while both sides develop. The g2-bishop's influence on the long diagonal is a constant theme, matched by Black's own fianchettoed bishop and pressure against d4 and c4.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: A principal line runs with cxd5 Nxd5, when White often plays Nf3 and develops harmoniously, aiming to build a broad centre with a later e4 while Black counters with ...c5, ...Nc6 and pressure on the d4-pawn. The resulting positions blend Grünfeld dynamism with the calmer manoeuvring of fianchetto systems.

Alternatively White can maintain the tension or support the centre, and Black can choose between recapturing on d5 or reinforcing with moves like ...c6 in more restrained treatments. Precise handling of the c4 and d5 squares is essential, as the opening rewards accurate move orders and understanding of when to release or hold the central tension.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Neo-Grünfeld emerged as players sought to combine the counterattacking spirit of the Grünfeld with the flexible King's-Indian fianchetto move order, avoiding some of White's most heavily analysed Grünfeld setups. It has become a sophisticated modern choice, favoured by those who value dynamic central play and rich strategic content over sharp forced theory.
